draft.title: The women's movement
card: From the 1960s, many women in Western countries began to campaign together for change. This is often called second-wave feminism. It built on earlier campaigns, such as the fight for the vote.
Women often earned less than men for similar work, and some laws treated them differently. Campaigners called for equal pay and for equal legal rights, such as in work, property and credit.
Campaigners also wanted more control over their own lives. This included access to contraception, choices about work and family, and protection from violence in the home.
Groups used protests, marches, public meetings, writing and court cases. In Australia, the Women's Electoral Lobby formed in 1972 to press political parties on women's issues.
draft.remember: The movement sought equal pay, equal legal rights and more say over women's own lives.

a.q: Which demand shows the women's movement seeking more control over women's own lives?
opts: Access to contraception and choices about family
A change to the age at which people can vote
Higher tariffs on goods imported from overseas
An end to rules that split schools by religion
a.why: Contraception and choices about family are decisions about a woman's own life, which campaigners wanted women to make. The vote is a tempting option, but the card places it in earlier campaigns, not the demands of the 1960s movement.
a.clue: Look for a choice a woman makes about her own life.

b.q: In 1975, Dana in Adelaide finds that her male co-worker is paid more for the same job. She joins a campaign to change this. Which demand is she supporting?
b.why: Being paid less than a man for the same work is the problem that the call for equal pay aimed to fix. The vote is tempting because it is a famous women's cause, but it belongs to earlier campaigns and has no link to pay.
b.clue: Her complaint is about wages for the same work.

a.best: Access to contraception and choices about family

problems.detail: The three distractors (voting age, schools split by religion, tariffs) have nothing to do with women, so a student can pick the right option without knowing the idea. Distractors drawn from the movement's other demands, such as equal pay, would test the distinction properly.

Why (a) treats the voting option as 'the vote' from earlier women's campaigns. The option actually says 'a change to the age at which people can vote', which is not the women's suffrage campaign, so the explanation misdescribes the distractor.
The clue 'Her complaint is about wages for the same work' all but states the answer, and it echoes the stem's 'paid more for the same job'. Little is left to reason out.

proposal.title: The women's movement
card: From the 1960s, many women in Western countries began to campaign together for change. This is often called second-wave feminism. It built on earlier campaigns, such as the fight for the vote.

Women often earned less than men for the same work, and some laws treated them unequally. Campaigners called for equal pay and for equal legal rights, such as owning property and getting credit in their own name.
Campaigners also wanted more control over their own lives. This included access to contraception, choices about having children, and protection from violence in the home.
Groups used protests, marches, public meetings, writing and court cases. In Australia, the Women's Electoral Lobby formed in 1972 to press political parties on women's issues.
proposal.remember: The movement sought equal pay, equal legal rights and more say over women's own lives.

a.q: Which demand was about women having more say over their own lives?
opts: Access to contraception so women could plan families
Equal pay for women doing the same work as men
Equal rights for women to get credit in their own name
Equal rights for married women to own property
a.why: Contraception let women decide whether and when to have children, a choice about their own lives. Equal pay and equal rights to credit or property are tempting, but the card groups them under pay and legal rights, not control over women's own lives.
a.clue: Which demand is about a choice in a woman's private life?

b.q: In 1975, Dana in Adelaide finds that her male co-worker is paid more for the same job. She joins a campaign to change this. Which demand is she supporting?
b.why: Being paid less than a man for the same work is the problem the call for equal pay aimed to fix. Equal rights to credit is tempting because it is also about money and fairness, but it concerns how the law treated women, not their wages.
b.clue: Think about what is different between Dana and her co-worker.
